title: Show HN: Sectr – Serverless backend platform for easy deployment of AI agents
author: donald_pinckney
body:
Hey HN, I've been building Sectr, a backend-as-a-service for making it easy(ier) to develop and deploy AI agents. Deploying agents requires non-trivial systems design work. Consider a support agent: how do you stream messages to your frontend, how/where do you persist messages for frontend fetching later (or for auditing), and when the agent wants to issue a refund, do you spin-down the compute infra while it's waiting on human approval? Sectr aims to be the serverless abstraction and platform to provide these systems for you.No sign-up needed to try using the dev server: curl -fsSL https://sectr.dev/install.sh | sh # Install CLI
 sectr init my-agent && cd my-agent # Starter code
 sectr dev # Dev server, with UI to test chatting

Sectr provides:- Streaming of every token, tool call and event, and persistence so they can be loaded fresh later.- Scaling up, and down to zero when the agent needs to wait, and resumption right to the suspended agent's state.- Human approved tools automatically use Sectr's suspension and resumption capabilities, no code needed from you.- AG-UI endpoint for any deployed agent so you can trivially hook up your frontend- Local dev server experience, so you can rapidly debug and iterate on your agent's behaviorAt the core, you can deploy any container image to Sectr as long as it implements a certain shaped HTTP endpoint. In practice, currently Sectr provides adapters to let you deploy your existing OpenAI Agents SDK, LangGraph, or Pydantic AI agents, with only 2 new lines of code: app = AgentApp(name="support")
 app.add_route("/chat", openai_agents(agent))

Certainly the hardest part of building Sectr was getting the resumption logic to be correct and invisible, across the Program State x Model Provider x Agent Framework matrix. For example, an earlier bug was when a model replied with text plus a tool call, Sectr would resume that as two separate messages, instead of one message with a text and tool part. This works, but breaks prompt caching (and might subtly change model behavior).Sectr is free during the beta (and can be tried locally without sign-up); I mainly want feedback, especially on dev & deployment experiences, any bugs, and what features would excite you.Introductory video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H-y3wynkKc0Docs: https://docs.sectr.dev

title: Show HN: Dinemic – self-hosted ingress across multiple providers (DNS, LB, TLS)
author: didijo
body:
Hey HN,
I recently published a project for running self hosted, highly available ingress for your infrastructure: authoritative DNS for your own domain, load balancers and network mesh, to expose your web apps. It started over a year ago as side project to handle several websites for clients and other side projects, and finished as the replacement cert-manager, external-dns and ingress that works without k8s, and is independent from single cloud/vps provider.It ended up as the HA platform, able to manage dozens of load balancers with TLS termination (and Let's Encrypt integration), DNS servers and full redundant mesh. The design goal from the beginning was to prepare a tool with minimized risk of single point of failure and independent from single hosting.It is running all my home lab, nextcloud, gitlab and production websites for clients for the few last months.Quick links for those who want to test:
https://dinemic.com - project page
https://console.dinemic.com - hosted control plane, if you want to test it with your own vps and domain, without setting up whole stack
https://gitlab.cloudover.io/dinemic/docs - project documentationIn high availability section of documentation you will also find concepts and design of its components and sample analysis of downtime when things go wrong with your infra.It is AGPL, so you can host also at your own. Self hosted version covers all functionality, with API and command line tools.

title: Show HN: Carmen – harness for reliable AI-written Metal kernels
author: utsav1033
body:
# utsav1033/carmen

An AI writes Apple Metal GPU kernels, a judge it can't fool proves them, and the winners run inside a real model: Qwen 2.5 0.5B decode 3% faster with identical output; 75/75 planted bugs caught.

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: utsav1033.github.io
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-09-24T19:44:26Z

## Languages

- Metal
- Python
- Shell

## Top Contributors

- utsav1033 (82 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 
 An LLM writes GPU kernels for Apple Silicon and carmen tests every one. 
 Then it measures whether a real model on a Mac actually gets faster. 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 TL;DR ·
 The CLI ·
 Try it ·
 The problem ·
 How it works ·
 Results ·
 What I learned 
 

## TL;DR

- **Most AI-kernel results are graded by a check that misses a lot.** I planted 75 realistic bugs in GPU kernels: the usual check caught 40. carmen's tests caught all 75.
- **The kernels that passed were also faster.** Claude's masked softmax ran **1.82× faster** than Apple's MLX (MLX does it in 3 steps, Claude's in 1), and add + rmsnorm **1.41×**.
- **But in a real model they barely mattered:** +2–3% on Qwen 0.5B, nothing on bigger models, because MLX already reads the model's weights about as fast as the Mac allows. What did speed up bigger models was speculative decoding, an existing mlx-lm feature carmen measured: 1.48× on Qwen 3B.

 

## The CLI

**The home screen:** what's been proven, the models you can speed up, and the kernels carmen has written.

 

**A model's page** (Qwen 2.5 3B): everything measured on it, and what you can run.

 

Run `carmen`, press `m`, pick a model: it shows what's been measured on it and what you can run, no API key needed.

## The problem

LLMs can write GPU kernels, but a kernel can pass a quick test and still be wrong. Most AI-kernel benchmarks try a
single input and accept any answer that's roughly close. So a kernel that works on 1,024 numbers but forgets the last
one when there are 1,025, or one whose answers are slightly off, still counts as correct
(one study found this kind of check misses most precision bugs).

And even a kernel that really is correct and faster on its own may not make the model any faster.
I wanted to know if an LLM could make a model on my Mac faster, and prove it.

## How carmen works

 

At its core it's a loop: Claude writes a Metal kernel, carmen tests it, and the fastest correct one is kept and
improved. Plenty of projects do that. The difference is that carmen doesn't trust the loop, because a plain loop
fools itself in three ways:

- **The tests miss bugs.** So carmen's tests are tested: I planted 75 realistic bugs in correct kernels.
 carmen caught all 75; the usual one-input check caught 40. Failures tell Claude exactly where it went wrong.
- **The model learns to pass the tests instead of being correct.** So part of the test set is hidden: inputs Claude
 never sees, for correctness and for speed. Without that, 30% of LLM kernel "wins" on Metal broke
 on inputs nobody had tested.
- **"Faster" doesn't mean the model gets faster.** So every win is timed against MLX's own fusion with error bars,
 then checked again inside a real model. That's how carmen found that kernels which win on their own barely move Qwen at all.

How the testing works →

## Results

Everything here ran on my M4 MacBook Pro (16 GB). Numbers in brackets are the range the real value is 95% likely to be in.

**Single kernels.** Claude beat MLX where MLX splits the work into several small steps. On matmul and attention, which Apple has already tuned heavily, it lost:

| kernel | MLX | carmen | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| masked softmax | 3 kernels | 1 fused kernel | **1.82×** |
| add + rmsnorm | 2 kernels | 1 fused kernel | **1.41×** |
| matmul | Apple's tuned kernel | 1 kernel | 0.93× |
| attention | Apple's tuned kernel | 1 kernel | 0.54× |

Against MLX's own automatic fusion (`mx.compile`), the first two are still 1.38× and 1.43×.

**In real models,** carmen's fused MLP kernels (tuned on 0.5B) mostly disappear, because MLX is already close to the fastest the Mac can go:

| Qwen 2.5, 4-bit | MLX | carmen | speedup | fastest possible* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5B | 214 tok/s | 220 tok/s | **1.02×** [1.01–1.02] | ~337 tok/s |
| 1.5B | 94 tok/s | 87 tok/s | 0.93× [0.93–0.95] | ~108 tok/s |
| 3B | 44 tok/s† | 42 tok/s | 0.95× [0.93–0.97] | ~53 tok/s |

 *Each new word means reading all of the model's weights from memory once. My M4 reads about 94 GB/s, so a 1.74 GB
model (3B) can't go much past ~53 words per second, however good the kernels are. On a quiet Mac MLX runs 3B at ~52 of 53; on 0.5B it's
at 214 of 337, which is where carmen's kernels still had room.
†This 3B run was on a busier Mac, so both sides are slower. The speedup compares them run by run, so it still holds. 

**Why fusion barely helped: Amdahl's law.** If you speed up only part of the work, the whole job gets faster only as
much as that part allows: speeding up a fraction *p* of the time by *s* gives an overall speedup of 1 / ((1 − *p*) + *p*/*s*).

- On **0.5B**, about 36% of each word's time is the part kernels can shrink (launches, small steps). Even making it free
 would cap out around 1.56×. carmen's kernels got 1.02×.
- On **3B**, that part is about 3%. Even infinitely fast kernels would give at most 1 / 0.97 ≈ **1.03×**.

 

**What did make bigger models faster: speculative decoding.**

- A small model guesses the next few words, and the big model checks them all in one go.
- So the big model reads its weights once for several words instead of once per word.
- It's a feature mlx-lm already has. carmen just measured it (`carmen levers`).
- carmen also tried compressing the model's memory of the conversation (the KV cache). That made things slower, or broke the output:

Decode speed in tokens per second, stock MLX → with the technique:

| technique | model | 512-token prompt | 8k-token prompt | output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| speculative decoding | 3B | 51.8 → 64.7 · **1.24×** [1.20–1.28] | 44.5 → 66.0 · **1.48×** [1.46–1.53] | same as stock |
| | 7B | 24.1 → 28.6 · **1.19×** [1.18–1.22] | 22.1 → 24.8 · **1.13×** [1.12–1.15] | same as stock |
| 8-bit KV cache | 3B | 51.8 → 48.7 · 0.93× [0.93–0.94] | 44.5 → 37.8 · 0.86× [0.83–0.89] | 98–99% same |
| | 7B | 24.1 → 23.6 · 0.98× [0.98–0.98] | 22.1 → 20.3 · 0.92× [0.91–0.92] | 95–98% same |
| 4-bit KV cache | 3B | | | broken |

 
 Notes on these numbers 

- Speculative decoding beats the speed limit (66 vs ~46 tok/s on 3B at 8k) because it reads the weights once for several words. It helps less on 7B because the 0.5B draft is accepted less often (46–52% of words vs 57–71%).
- The 8-bit KV cache is slower because MLX runs attention on it as four separate steps instead of one fused kernel. That's carmen's next target.
- The 4-bit KV cache turns Qwen's output into gibberish ("The skyuser\nquiv"): its attention keys have outliers 4 bits can't hold.
- The "fastest possible" figures use my measured ~94 GB/s, which is a bit low (7B actually runs slightly faster than its figure), so treat them as approximate.
- Spec output matches stock until a late fp16 rounding flip, as expected when the big model checks words in a batch.

 

## What I learned

- AI kernels don't beat hand-tuned code. They beat code nobody fused.
- A kernel that wins alone can lose inside a model.
- Past ~1B parameters, memory is the limit, not kernels.
- Getting numbers I could trust took more work than writing the kernels.

New to this? How it all works explains LLMs, GPUs and kernels from scratch.

## Try it

On an Apple Silicon Mac:

```bash
pip install carmen-kernels          # or: uv tool install carmen-kernels
carmen                              # the app
carmen speedup                      # Qwen 2.5 0.5B, stock vs carmen's kernels, on your Mac (no API key)
carmen speedup qwen0.5b qwen3b      # several models in turn, then one table side by side
carmen levers qwen3b                # speculative decoding, KV cache quantization, 3-bit weights vs stock (no API key)
carmen key                          # only to cook new kernels: paste an Anthropic key once, saved for you only
```

 
 All commands 

| command | what it does |
|---|---|
| `carmen` | the terminal app: what's proven, speed up a model, pick a kernel, watch it cook |
| `carmen speedup [models…]` | stock MLX vs `mx.compile` vs carmen's bundled kernels on real models, taking turns; no API key (`--quick` for ~2 min a model) |
| `carmen levers [model]` | speculative decoding, 8/4-bit KV cache and 3-bit weights vs stock, at 512 and 8k prompts, with drift scored for the lossy ones; no API key |
| `carmen run [--for qwen0.5b]` | let Claude write one kernel; `--for` tests it at a real model's sizes |
| `carmen broken ` | plant bugs and check carmen's tests catch every one, next to the usual one-size check |
| `carmen judge ` | test a kernel you wrote |
| `carmen e2e [model]` | run a real model stock vs with carmen's kernels: speed, noise range, same answers? |
| `carmen profile [model]` | where a model spends its time, step by step |
| `carmen bench` | the feedback loop vs plain best-of-N, same budget |

 

From source: `git clone https://github.com/utsav1033/carmen`, then `pip install -e '.[dev]'`. Keys go in `carmen key`, a `.env` in the folder you run from, or your shell; the shell wins.

Control where original values may travel.** When protection is applied to a `ChatClient`, PII detected by analyzers is replaced with request-scoped tokens before the input is sent to the model. Immediately before a protected tool runs, original values are restored only for the entity types allowed by policy, and the tool result is protected again. Final-response inspection can be enabled when needed. Spring AI Privacy Guardrails combines a Spring-independent privacy `core` with Spring AI integration to enforce privacy policies across chat, RAG, memory, tool-call, and output boundaries. ## Why It Exists Detection is the first step. This library turns findings from built-in and pluggable analyzers into request-scoped policy at the model, tool, and output boundaries. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Input · Memory · RAG"] --> B["PII detection"] B --> C["core policy
validation · normalization · tokenization"] C --> D["Model boundary"] D -. "Tool call" .-> E["Tool boundary
restore only allowed originals"] E -. "Re-protected result" .-> D D --> F["Output boundary"] F --> G["Application"] ``` ## Run the Sample The sample includes a deterministic local `ChatModel`, so no cloud credentials are required. With JDK 17 installed, run the following command from the repository root: ```bash ./gradlew :spring-ai-privacy-guardrails-sample-demo:run ``` Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080` to use the sample's **Privacy Boundary Inspector**. Its views render runtime evidence returned by the sample backend: - **Local Tool** shows detected raw values replaced with opaque request-scoped tokens at the model boundary, only the allowed `CUSTOMER_ID` restored at the tool boundary, and the tool result protected again before model re-entry. - **RAG** compares the raw retrieved document with the protected context actually recorded at the model boundary. - **MCP** demonstrates the same scoped disclosure and result re-protection through a real local Streamable HTTP MCP round trip. Text not matched by the demo's detection rules may be returned unchanged by the local model, and the Inspector does not expose token mappings. title: Show HN: Markdown is 40× more token-efficient with SQLite
author: richardcrng
body: Hi HN, I'm Richard, founder of Native. I'm working on open-source context ownership, to stop AI centralisation: https://github.com/withnative/nativeMy first focus has been making Markdown vaults powerful enough so that teams can self-host all of their context (messaging, docs and projects), without it being externally fragmented or rate-limited.I'm sharing some early results: Markdown vaults can be 40× more efficient with SQLite!https://www.withnative.ai/research-and-posts/markdown-contex...Here's some of the main ideas:- SQLite or Markdown folders, you pick. You can project the same authoritative event log into either form; more projection formats will follow (e.g. maybe neo4j; we do use a graph structure).- Empirically: SQLite is better for agents! On a 120 trial evaluation for 11,000 records, agents use 40× fewer tokens with SQLite vs Markdown, per correct answer.- Everything is a file or SQLite row. Messages, documents and projects: all can be modelled in your vault. You get local-first collaboration with teammates, synced to a cloud of your choice.- You can render your vault with arbitrary UI. Your WhatsApp-like UI speaks to your teammate's Slack-like UI; both are just views over the same database.A few things I've learned building this:- Agents do pretty well even without SQL if you give them strongly typed Markdown frontmatter. This was one arm of the trial I ran. I didn't have any clear expectations, but it was cool to watch: agents ended up writing Python scripts to do SQL-like queries.- Cumulatively, cached input tokens can get expensive. I feel silly in hindsight here. I'd gotten used to letting my sessions run long, "It's all cached so it's very cheap". But when I looked at my results here, over 2/3 of the token bill on long sessions was cached input...- "Markdown vaults don't scale as well as databases" isn't as self-evident as I think. This is why I decided to benchmark it... I've had some very blank stares when I try to explain how Markdown files might break at true agent-scale volume.Unfortunately, the dataset is private, because it's two months of my own work. I am considering open-sourcing it even so, but there is definitely some embarrassing stuff in there. TBD... I know that independent result verification matters!The core engine that I evaluated is open-source, with more to be released soon: https://github.com/withnative/nativeIf you're interested in trying connected context on an open engine, you can get updates from our website or email me directly: richard@withnative.aihttps://www.withnative.ai/

title: Show HN: ssh zydra.sh, a GPU Linux desktop in your terminal, with Doom
author: teledream
body:
ssh zydra.shThere's no sign-up or anything, and you get a 15-minute demo of a graphical Linux VM drawn entirely in your terminal. It has a browser, an editor, and it runs Doom.It works best in Kitty or Ghostty. WezTerm and Konsole also work, as well as Sixel and iTerm2 terminals, though with less detail. Text-only terminals support non-graphical apps: shells, editors, and other TUIs.Why? For a few months I ran coding agents in tmux on a VPS over SSH, and it sucked. I couldn't paste images, scrolling broke and I didn't wanna figure out why, I had no notifications for when an agent finished, I couldn't see browsers agents opened to smoke-test, logins drifted between my laptop and the server, I couldn't check in from my phone, and to know what an agent had done five minutes ago I had to read through opaque chunks of tool calls. These issues added up and had me in a limbo: They made my setup bad enough to annoy me every day, but not quite bad enough to stop my real work and fix it.How it works: Zydra is a custom (Smithay-based) Wayland compositor in a microVM with an AMD GPU, implementing a series of terminal protocols that solve many issues but are often ignored: Kitty graphics for windows, OSC 52 for the clipboard, images included, OSC 9/99/777 for notifications, SGR mouse for scrolling and clicks. VNC is limited to sending pictures of the screen and diffing frames to find what changed. In Zydra, apps directly tell the compositor what changed, and terminal text is sent as text you can select and copy natively. The browser is a WebKit build that delivers frames to the compositor as DMA-BUFs without a readback, and agents drive it through Playwright. Alt+P is sort of like Raycast: browse apps, linked GitHub, websites, and SSH targets from it.You can watch the desktop at any point in time and rewind to periodic snapshots. To achieve this, the desktop records into a timeline file, a kind of structured video, and the VM takes snapshots along it. You can traverse back like a livestream to see what happened while you were away, then restore or fork the whole machine from that point. Agents can mark points on the timeline and checkpoint the whole machine before risky changes.Other things to try: ssh -t zydra.sh dino # the Chromium dino game via SSH
 tar -czf - -C ~ .claude .claude.json | ssh -T zydra.sh upload # bring your configs (includes your Claude login)
 ssh -o ObscureKeystrokeTiming=no -A zydra.sh # lower latency & forward your SSH agent
 ssh -p 443 zydra.sh # connect from a corporate firewall
 sshfs zydra.sh: ~/zydra # paid accounts: mount your home

Everything runs on one dedicated server with one AMD iGPU, so there are 12 demo slots. When they're full you wait in a queue and can play Chromium's offline dino game. The paid plan is $40/month (+ tax): 8 GB RAM, 4 vCPUs, 80 GB disk, GPU access, with no time limit and a 3-day money-back guarantee.I'll be around all day to answer questions.

(your VPS or managed cloud)"] H["Web UI · board · proxy"] end subgraph yours["Machines you own (behind NAT/firewall)"] W1["Worker: terminals · agents · apps"] W2["Worker: terminals · agents · apps"] end B -->|HTTPS| H W1 -.->|"dials OUT (WSS)"| H W2 -.->|"dials OUT (WSS)"| H ``` ## What it does **Persistent terminals, one browser tab away.** Real PTYs on your machines — your login shell, your dotfiles, true color — that survive closing the laptop, network drops, and hub restarts. Reattach from any browser, including your phone (with a touch key bar for ctrl/esc/arrows). Two people can attach to the same live terminal. If you live in tmux: sessions map to *spaces*, panes to side-by-side terminals, and *space definitions* (saved layout + working dir + command per pane) respawn your setup on demand — an alternative, not a drop-in replacement (no tmux keybindings or copy-mode). Files move without `scp`: a **files** menu on the space browses the machine, downloads a file or a whole folder (videos, PDFs, images and logs also open in a tab), and takes drops to upload; `cordane get report.pdf` typed in a terminal offers that file to whoever may download it. Owner-only unless you say otherwise. **A board that runs the work.** Drop a ticket on the kanban board and Cordane cuts a git worktree, boots the dev server on its own port, and turns your coding agent loose — while the whole team watches live. Or give the ticket a start time — 07:00, in *your* time zone, not the server's — and it runs itself overnight, so the branch and the diff are waiting when you sit down. Review a diff and a green-checks badge, then merge — from your phone if that's where you are. Not right yet? **Request changes**: write what to fix, click lines of the diff to pin notes to them, and send it back — to the agent in the ticket's space (the same session, if the space is still open) or as a background pass on the same branch. A project can also send failing checks back to the agent on its own: the failing commands and the tail of their output, up to a retry budget you set (off by default), after which the ticket waits in review for you. Review on GitHub instead? A *changes requested* on the PR becomes the same kind of round, read with the worker's own `gh` and only from the repo's collaborators. Anything the agent leaves in `.cordane/outputs/` — a screenshot of the feature, a report — is attached to the ticket when its run ends. Agents know both channels without being told: the hub installs a skill on every worker that Claude Code, Codex, opencode and pi read at session start. Every run keeps its full audit trail: exact prompt, exact diff, what checks ran. Keep your tracker — this is the execution layer where agent work happens, not a project-management tool. Tickets come in from **Sentry, Jira, GitHub Issues or Linear** (paste an issue URL, or let a filter create them), and the upstream issue is closed when the ticket is done. **More than one agent, more than one ticket.** A ticket can wait on others (*blocked by*), and a plan too big for one pass splits into sub-tickets that can run one after another. Not sure which agent will do it best? **Race** two or three on the same ticket — each in its own worktree on its own branch — compare their diffs and checks side by side, and keep the winner. **Detect from repo** reads your manifests on the worker and proposes the setup, start and check hooks, so a new project doesn't start from a blank form. **Told when it matters, and what it cost.** An agent stuck on a permission prompt, a failed run, a plan waiting for approval, work ready for review: Cordane tells the person whose agent it is — in the browser, through a webhook (presets for ntfy, Slack and Discord), or by email when the hub has SMTP. Agents can speak up mid-run too: `cordane mcp` gives the agent working a ticket tools to read it, comment, file a follow-up, attach a file or flag it for a human. Each headless run records the usage its agent CLI reports — tokens, and cost from Claude Code and opencode — and a per-project **Insights** page shows runs, success rate, time and spend by agent. **Terminals an agent — or your laptop — can drive.** In a space, the same `cordane mcp` server lets an agent work the space's other terminals: run a command and get back its output and exit code, type keys, wait for output, or hand the agent in another pane a task. It reaches only its own space, and by default an agent working a ticket imported from Sentry, Jira, Linear or GitHub — or one that has read such a ticket — may only read its neighbours. With a personal API token (**Settings → API tokens**), an MCP client on your laptop — Claude Code or Cursor over `https:// /api/v1/mcp`, Claude Desktop by signing in — can start and stop spaces, define layouts, run worker apps, share spaces and drive their terminals. Admins can turn tokens off or limit them to admins; terminal input is written to the audit log. **Preview links without a tunnel.** Apps on a worker get a stable subdomain (`myapp--worker.your-domain`) served through the worker's outbound connection — no ngrok, no rotating hostnames, no per-seat paywall. Auth on by default; flip an app to **Public** to share it with anyone, no account needed. Ticket previews stay team-only. (For sharing previews — Cordane is not an inbound tunnel for webhooks.) **Teams on your terms.** GitHub sign-in with an admin-managed allowlist, projects shared across a team, each member running work on their own private worker. Self-host the hub on a $5 VPS, or use the managed cloud (`your-team.cordane.app`) — workers stay on your hardware either way. Your code, secrets, and compute never leave machines you control. ## See it One short video per feature, nothing staged — the agent output is whatever the model produced on the day it was filmed. | | | |---|---| | Close your laptop, keep your shell · 1:26 | a process on your machine survives a closed tab **and a hub restart** — timestamps prove it | | Handing a ticket to a coding agent · 3:36 | Plan cuts a worktree and hands Claude Code the ticket; the plan lands back on the card | | Self-hosting a worker · 1:16 | one command behind NAT, then `ss -ltnp` shows it listens on nothing | | Port forwards — no ngrok · 3:20 | a stable link for any port, and a share link that needs no account | | Cordane on a phone · 0:35 | the whole hub, not a cut-down app — a PR reviewed and merged from a phone | All of them, by topic: @cordanehq. How it works under the hood: One outbound WebSocket. ## How it's built - **One Go binary, two roles**: `cordane server` (hub) and `cordane worker`. - **Workers dial out** over WebSocket; the hub never connects in. Nothing to port-forward, nothing inbound to firewall. - **SQLite** for all hub state — trivial backups (built-in Litestream replication to any S3-compatible bucket), no database server, easy export. - Joining a machine is one command: ```sh cordane worker join https://your-team.cordane.app --token crdjt_… ``` ## Try it on your machine One command, no server, no DNS, no GitHub app: ```sh curl -fsSL https://cordane.ai/install.sh | sh # the `cordane` binary (Linux, macOS) cordane up ``` Or both in one go, which also works before `~/.local/bin` is on your `PATH`: `curl -fsSL https://cordane.ai/install.sh | sh -s up`. `cordane up` starts a hub on `localhost` with this machine as its worker, signs you in, and opens the board in your browser. It's a single-user hub that listens only on loopback: sign-in links come from the terminal (`cordane login` prints a fresh one), and app previews open at `http:// --.localhost:8080` in Chrome, Firefox or Edge (`--path-previews` covers Safari). Everything lives in `~/.cordane-local`, so `rm -rf ~/.cordane-local` starts over. Terminals and agents run while the command does, and Ctrl-C stops them; `cordane up --install-service` keeps it running in the background instead (a systemd user service or launchd agent that starts at login). When you want it on your phone, for a team, or always on, self-host a hub (below) or use managed cloud. Your machine stays the worker either way. ## Self-hosting Two containers on one small VPS: the hub, plus Caddy for automatic TLS. Images are public on GHCR, so you need nothing installed but Docker. First point a DNS `A` record for your hub's hostname (e.g. `cordane.example.com`) at the box. ```sh git clone https://github.com/cordane/cordane.git cd cordane/deploy cp .env.example .env # fill in the values below, then: docker compose up -d docker compose logs -f # both containers; Ctrl-C once the hub is listening ``` Five values in `.env` get you running — your hub's URL, a secret key, and a GitHub OAuth app's id/secret for sign-in: | Var | What | |-----|------| | `EXTERNAL_URL` / `CONTROL_HOST` | your hub's URL / hostname | | `CORDANE_SECRET_KEY` | `openssl rand -base64 32` — **back this up** | | `CORDANE_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID/SECRET` | a GitHub OAuth app (create one): homepage = your `EXTERNAL_URL`, callback `${EXTERNAL_URL}/api/v1/auth/github/callback`; then *Generate a new client secret* | That's simple mode: one hostname, a normal certificate, previews at `/w/{worker}/{app}/`. Wildcard preview subdomains need a DNS API token — switching is three lines in `.env`, see `deploy/README.md`. Open your `EXTERNAL_URL` and sign in with GitHub — **the first account to sign in becomes the admin**, so do it right away. Then connect a machine: ```sh curl -fsSL https:///install.sh | sh # installs the `cordane` binary cordane worker join https:// --token crdjt_… # token from the hub's Workers page ``` `join` enrolls the machine and keeps running as the worker; to keep it up after you log out, run it under systemd/launchd (`cordane worker run` — see `deploy/README.md`). ### Your first agent run 1. **On the worker**, install the agent you want and sign in once in a normal terminal — e.g. `claude` (Claude Code), `codex`, `opencode` or `pi`. Cordane drives the agent that's there; it doesn't bring its own login. 2. **New project**: pick your worker and a repo (an SSH/HTTPS URL it can clone, or a checkout already on the worker). For implementing, tick **Allow the agent to run commands** — off by default, because a background (headless) implement runs the agent without permission prompts. 3. **New ticket** → **▶ Plan**: the ticket's space opens with the agent working. When the plan lands, **✓ Approve → Implement**. These buttons drive the agent live in the space, so it asks you there for any permission it needs — answer in the pane (or set the project's agent command to skip them, e.g. `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions`). When the agent finishes, the ticket moves to review with its diff, and a PR if the worker has `gh`. Backups to any S3-compatible bucket and the wildcard mode are in `deploy/README.md`. **No license key required.** The Community tier — 1 worker, 1 project, 2 users, 3 concurrent agent runs, and *every* feature — is free forever and makes no license calls; the only request a keyless hub sends us is an update check (release channel name only — `CORDANE_UPDATE_CHECK=off` turns it off). Paid keys lift the caps and keep working offline within a grace window, so a Cordane outage never blocks you. See pricing. ## Issues & feedback This is Cordane's public home — bug reports and feature requests are welcome in Issues. For anything security-related, see SECURITY.md. ## License The contents of **this repository** — documentation and deployment configuration — are MIT-licensed (LICENSE). Copy, fork and adapt them freely. The **container images** they deploy (`ghcr.io/cordane/cordane`, `ghcr.io/cordane/caddy`) are proprietary software owned by Sitedity SRL, free to run on the Community tier and otherwise governed by the Terms. `NOTICE` spells out the split. # saftacatalinmihai/lcars

# spapas/tiny-tube

A tine tube like service

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 1
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: master
- Created: 2026-10-13T19:10:43Z

## Languages

- Batchfile
- Go
- HTML
- JavaScript

## Top Contributors

- spapas (31 contributions)

---

## README

# Tiny Tube

CI

Tiny Tube is a self-hosted video-sharing server for training videos,
presentations, and recorded meetings. It runs as a single Go binary, with an
embedded web interface, SQLite metadata, and video files stored on disk.

- **One binary:** runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. No separate database server
 or frontend setup is required.
- **A searchable video library:** categories, sorting, playback speed controls,
 and original-file downloads, with an English and Greek interface.
- **Optional HLS and posters:** add FFmpeg for conversion and preview images.
 Without it, play original files in browsers that support their codecs.
- **Local or LDAP login:** editors upload and edit; administrators also delete
 videos and manage users. Roles are assigned locally.
- **Public viewing or locked lists:** share a group of videos through a secret
 link. Anyone with the link can view that list; editors and administrators can
 access all videos for management.

Download a release ·
Installation · Configuration ·
HTTP API · License

Run one server process per video directory. HLS currently provides a single
720p rendition; backups, storage quotas, and adaptive quality are not built in.
See the review and remaining limitations
for deployment details.

## Screenshots

The examples below use demonstration content.

**Library:** browse by category, search, and sort videos by date, views, or title.

Video library with category filters and title sorting

**Watch:** play a video, adjust playback speed, and share or download the original.

Video watch page with playback controls and video details

**Upload:** add a video and choose its title, category, description, and visibility.

Video upload form and visibility options

## Installation

### 1. Download and extract

Download the archive for your system from GitHub Releases:
Windows (`.zip`), Linux, or macOS (`.tar.gz`), choosing `amd64` for Intel/AMD
or `arm64` for ARM, including Apple Silicon. Extract it and open a terminal in
the extracted folder. The binaries are unsigned; Windows or macOS may show a
security prompt.

The release contains the server, the `tiny-tube-cli` administration tool,
configuration examples, documentation, and `VERSION.txt`. Go and a separate
database server are not required: SQLite and the web interface are included.
You need a writable video directory with space for originals and generated media.

To verify the download, compare its hash with the matching filename in the
release's `SHA256SUMS`. For example, for the v1.0.3 amd64 archives:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
Get-FileHash .\tiny-tube-v1.0.3-windows-amd64.zip -Algorithm SHA256
```

```sh
# Linux
sha256sum tiny-tube-v1.0.3-linux-amd64.tar.gz
# macOS (use darwin-arm64 for Apple Silicon)
shasum -a 256 tiny-tube-v1.0.3-darwin-amd64.tar.gz
```

Use the filename for the version and platform you downloaded.

### 2. Configure the first administrator

For a **new installation**, copy `.env.example` to `.env` in the extracted folder:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
Copy-Item .env.example .env
```

```sh
# Linux / macOS
cp .env.example .env
```

Open `.env` in a text editor and set `ADMIN_PASS` to a strong password. The
default administrator name is `admin`; change `ADMIN_USER` if you prefer.
The password cannot be empty or `changeme`. Keep `.env` private: it may contain
credentials. Do not replace an existing `.env` when upgrading.

### 3. Start the server

From that same extracted folder, run:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
.\tiny-tube.exe
```

```sh
# Linux / macOS
./tiny-tube
```

Open on the same computer. Sign in with the administrator
credentials, then use **Upload video** to add a video or **Administration** to
manage users. Press `Ctrl+C` in the terminal to stop the server.

On the first start with an empty user table, Tiny Tube creates the administrator.
After that, manage users and passwords at `/admin`; changing `ADMIN_USER` or
`ADMIN_PASS` does not change existing accounts. The library starts empty. By
default, videos and the SQLite database are stored in `videos/` under the
working directory.

For HLS conversion and automatically generated posters, install FFmpeg separately
with the `libx264` and AAC encoders, and make it available on `PATH` (or set
`FFMPEG_BIN`). Without FFmpeg, original-file playback remains available when the
browser supports the video's format and codecs.

The default address only accepts local connections. For network access, configure
the address and HTTPS; see Configuration and the Nginx example.
Plan backups of the videos and database; Tiny Tube does not create them
automatically. See Security and remaining limitations.

For a long-running Linux deployment, configure a service with the intended
working directory, absolute `VIDEO_DIR`, and credentials. If conversion is
needed, ensure the service can find FFmpeg. A systemd unit is not included.

For operator role fixes without the web UI, the release's `tiny-tube-cli`
provides `users list` and `users set-role --username U --role admin|editor|viewer`.
Use the same `VIDEO_DIR`, `STORE`, and `DB_PATH` settings as the server. The CLI
refuses to demote the last active administrator.

## Locked lists

Public videos stay visible to everyone. For sensitive material, an
administrator creates any number of locked lists at `/admin/lists`,
each with its own long random key. Uploads and edits
offer a visibility picker: public by default, or one locked list per video.
Existing videos stay public unless moved.

- Holders of `/view_list?key=…` see exactly that list; without the key its
 videos are excluded from the library, search, category counts, and API listings.
 Direct requests for their watch page, metadata, originals, HLS segments, or
 posters return 404 unless an unlock cookie or editor/administrator access applies.
- The first key visit sets an unlock cookie so posters, HLS segments and
 later pages keep working without repeating the key.
- Editors and administrators see every video without a key, so lost links
 never block management.
- A link is a bearer credential: anyone it is forwarded to gains access.
 Share links only over a safe channel. Rotating the key
 revokes every copy at once, including previously granted cookies.
 Deleting a list is refused while it still holds videos, so videos cannot
 silently become public.
- The Nginx sample proxies every route through Go, so the same checks apply
 behind the proxy.
- Missing/unreadable metadata never authorizes media access. Orphan files without
 metadata return 404; recover their metadata before sharing them.
- Visibility changes are synchronized with media authorization. Failed list-picker
 loads block upload/edit forms. An API edit omitting `access_list` preserves
 visibility; send an explicit empty value to make a video public.
- Copy Link offers a locked-video URL only when its valid list key is present.
 Otherwise the page explains that the original locked-list link is required.

For scripts, pass the key as `?key=…` on `/api/videos`, `/api/video`,
`/watch` and `/videos/…`, or reuse the unlock cookie from a link visit.

## Configuration

The server loads `.env` from its working directory. Explicit environment variables
take precedence, including empty values. Values may be quoted; there is no variable
expansion or inline-comment support. `.env` is ignored by Git.

| Variable | Default | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VIDEO_DIR` | `videos` | Video storage; relative paths use the process working directory. |
| `ADDR` | unset | Full `host:port` bind address, overriding `HOST` and `PORT`. Default effective address is `127.0.0.1:8081`. |
| `HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | Bind host when `ADDR` is unset. Set `0.0.0.0` explicitly for IPv4 network access. |
| `PORT` | `8081` | HTTP port when `ADDR` is unset; `PORT=8080` remains supported. |
| `STORE` | `sqlite` | Metadata backend: `sqlite` or legacy `fs`. Video files remain on disk in both modes. |
| `DB_PATH` | `<VIDEO_DIR>/tiny-tube.db` | SQLite metadata database in WAL mode. Relative paths use the working directory. |
| `ADMIN_USER` | `admin` | First administrator, created on first boot when no users exist. Ignored afterwards. |
| `ADMIN_PASS` | required on first boot | Password for the first administrator; startup rejects an unset/blank password or `changeme` when the user table is empty. |
| `AUTH_MODE` | `local` | Login source: `local`, `ldap`, or `both`. In `both`, existing local accounts use their local password directly; other identities use LDAP. LDAP never adopts same-named local accounts, roles or keys. |
| `COOKIE_SECURE` | `false` | Set `true` behind HTTPS so session cookies carry the Secure flag. |
| `LDAP_ADDR` | `ldap://localhost:389` | Directory address (`ldap://` or `ldaps://`). |
| `LDAP_BASE_DN` | `dc=example,dc=com` | Fallback search base and direct-bind default. |
| `LDAP_BIND_DN` | unset | Service account for subtree search; without it, users bind directly. |
| `LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD` | unset | Service account password. |
| `LDAP_SEARCH_BASES` | unset | `;`-separated search bases enabling subtree search. |
| `LDAP_USER_FILTER` | `(uid=%s)` | Search filter with the escaped username as `%s`. |
| `LDAP_USER_DN` | `uid=%s, ` | Direct-bind DN template for the username. |
| `LDAP_ATTR_EMAIL` | `mail` | Directory attribute mapped to the user record. |
| `LDAP_ATTR_FIRST_NAME` | `givenName` | Directory attribute for the display name. |
| `LDAP_ATTR_LAST_NAME` | `sn` | Directory attribute for the display name. |
| `LDAP_ALWAYS_UPDATE` | `true` | Refresh LDAP user records from the directory on every login. |
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | `2147483648` | Maximum **whole multipart request**, including form fields and overhead: 2 GiB. Larger requests return HTTP 413. |
| `TRANSCODE_WORKERS` | `1` | Maximum concurrent FFmpeg processes, between 1 and 16. Pending jobs remain on disk. |
| `AUTH_REQUESTS_PER_MINUTE` | `60` | Protected-route requests per source IP per minute, checked before authentication; 1–3600. Excess requests return 429 with `Retry-After`. |
| `UPLOAD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `1800` | Total authenticated multipart read deadline; 1–86400 seconds. Stalled uploads return 408 and are cleaned up. |
| `TRANSCODE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `1800` | Total HLS/poster conversion deadline; 1–86400 seconds. Expired jobs become `failed`, preserving originals. |
| `FFMPEG_BIN` | unset | Explicit executable path/name, preferred over `PATH`. An invalid explicit value fails startup. Otherwise FFmpeg is discovered on `PATH`. |

Empty optional values fall back to the defaults. For direct LAN access, set `HOST`
explicitly (or set `ADDR=0.0.0.0:8081`) and configure the firewall. Session cookies
need HTTPS when used over a network; the Go server itself serves HTTP. Video files
and public metadata are public. Login sessions last 24 hours sliding, with expiry
and the browser cookie renewed at most once per five minutes of activity. Refresh
only updates live sessions and cannot recreate a revoked token. Password resets,
deactivation and user deletion revoke sessions. Unlock cookies are session
cookies signed per process and die with the browser session or a restart;
reopening the list link restores them.

When upgrading an older build that automatically adopted local usernames into
LDAP, review its existing LDAP role grants. The new login path prevents future
adoption but preserves existing accounts/roles; it does not reconstruct their
previous authentication source.

Browser mutations must originate from this site. Cross-origin upload/edit/delete
requests return 403, including JSON clients; command-line clients without browser
origin headers continue to work. Changing `Accept`/`format=json` does not bypass
authentication, request limits or origin protection. CSP blocks inline scripts
and embedding the interface in frames; MIME sniffing is disabled.

The auth limit uses the actual socket source address and ignores forwarding
headers. Behind Nginx, clients share its IP bucket: tune the Go aggregate limit
and apply per-client limits at the trusted edge. Public viewing/API reads remain
available during an auth cooldown. Limiter memory is bounded.

Headers have a 10-second timeout and a 64 KiB limit. Ordinary request reads are
limited to 30 seconds; authenticated uploads use their separate configured
deadline. Response writes are limited to `max(30 minutes, UPLOAD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS
+ 60 seconds)`, so unusually slow original downloads may need a larger setting.

## Upload and playback

The interface supports English and Greek on every page, including administration,
upload validation and player messages. Use the language selector in the header;
the choice is saved in a browser cookie for one year and works without JavaScript.
Until a choice is saved, the browser's `Accept-Language` preference selects a
supported language; unsupported preferences fall back to English. Switching preserves the
current page, search/filter/pagination parameters and locked-list key.
Switching reloads the page, so save edits or finish an upload first.
Dates, file sizes and view/video counts follow the selected language. Titles,
descriptions, categories, list names and other user content retain their original
text. JSON API fields, status values, errors, server logs and CLI output retain
their existing format/language for automation.

English is the source catalog in `web/locales/en.json`; `el.json` translates the
same stable message IDs (for example `upload.title`). The server uses `go-i18n`
for named variables and CLDR plural rules, and `golang.org/x/text` for language
matching and number formatting. Browser messages use the same catalogs, with
`Intl.PluralRules` and `Intl.NumberFormat`; CSP needs no inline exceptions.
Missing translations fall back to English. To add another language, add its
standard go-i18n JSON catalog with a `language.name` entry and rebuild: discovery,
cookies, negotiation and the selector automatically include it. No Go/HTML/JS
language lists need editing. See the translation guide for examples,
plural forms and validation. No frontend packages are required.

The interface defaults to light mode. The theme button switches between light and
dark and remembers the selection in browser-local storage; it does not follow the
operating system's theme automatically. Library, watch, and upload pages adapt to
mobile, tablet, and desktop screens. Categories can be combined with text search.
Library and locked-list pages show 24 videos by default, with Previous/Next
navigation preserving search, category and sort. Long visibility labels fit narrow
screens. Administrator deletion confirmations apply to every row and identify
whether a video, user or list is being deleted.

The upload page supports file selection or drag-and-drop, shows the chosen file,
and reports upload progress and errors without discarding the form. Without
JavaScript, its standard multipart form still works. The watch page provides link
copying and access to the original file. The interface uses restrained colors and
task-oriented wording for workplace use. Cards display an extracted poster when
available and a neutral placeholder otherwise. The player offers speeds from
0.5× to 2× and attempts playback with sound; where the browser blocks
it, the viewer presses play. The video is never muted.

The watch page links to `/edit?id= ` and provides deletion with a confirmation
prompt. `GET /edit` and `POST /api/edit` require an editor or administrator login;
`POST /api/delete` and `/admin` require an administrator. The watch page shows
management actions only to users holding the matching role. Editing changes title/description/category/visibility while
preserving playback data. Deletion cancels and waits for active conversion, then
removes the original, HLS, poster and metadata. There is no undo.

Each authorized watch-page load counts one view, debounced to one per viewer
address per video every 24 hours so refreshes do not inflate totals; denied
requests never count. Totals appear on library cards and the watch page, and
the library and locked-list pages offer most-viewed and title sorts alongside
the default recency order. Title sorting is case-insensitive and orders numbers
naturally, so Lesson 2 comes before Lesson 10. The library and API accept
`sort=views` or `sort=title`; paging and filters preserve the selection.

1. An authenticated `POST /api/upload` accepts multipart fields `title` (required),
 `desc`, `category`, and `file`.
2. The original is saved to `VIDEO_DIR/ /`. Recognized filename extensions are
 `.mp4`, `.mov`, `.mkv`, and `.webm`; unsupported extensions or mismatched
 container signatures return HTTP 415. This is a basic header check, not full
 codec/file validation. Titles are limited to 512 bytes, descriptions to 8,192,
 and categories to 256. A unique directory is reserved for each upload, and
 incomplete uploads are removed if saving the original or metadata fails.
3. If FFmpeg is available, metadata starts as `queued`. A bounded worker marks it
 `processing`, generates HLS in a staging directory, and publishes it only after
 FFmpeg succeeds and produces a complete playlist. A JPEG poster is extracted
 at one second, falling back to the first frame; poster failure is non-fatal.
 Status then becomes `ready`.
 Without FFmpeg, status is immediately `ready` for original-file playback.
4. Reload the watch page after conversion to use HLS. Safari can use native HLS;
 other supported browsers use hls.js, with original-file fallback when HLS
 support is unavailable or HLS playback fails. The page uses the vendored
 hls.js 1.6.19 (`web/static/hls.min.js`, Apache-2.0, see `hls.js.LICENSE.txt`);
 no external browser access is required.
5. Conversion failures become `failed`, with a visible message and the original
 retained. Pending/interrupted jobs resume on startup if FFmpeg is available;
 otherwise they become `failed`. On graceful shutdown, active conversions are
 cancelled and requeued. Failed jobs are not automatically retried.

## HTTP API

`GET /api/videos` is paginated: use `page` (starting at 1) and `page_size`
(default 50, maximum 100; HTML defaults to 24). Responses include `total`
(visible library size), `filtered` (matching visible videos), `count` (items on
this page), `page`, `page_size`, `pages` and `items`. Clients that assumed one
request returned every video must iterate through the pages. Out-of-range positive
pages resolve to the last page; invalid/oversized parameters return 400.
Authorization applies before counts, category totals or paging. SQLite filters
and pages in queries, retaining Greek search and precise date ordering; legacy
FS still scans JSON records. Readiness and conversion polling use lightweight
SQLite queries. View debounce memory has a hard 8,192-entry cap; eviction can
permit an extra view under heavy churn.

Programmatic clients log in with `POST /api/login` (`{"username", "password"}`)
and reuse the session cookie, exactly like a browser. For scripts that should
not juggle cookies, an administrator can issue a long-lived API key per user
at `/admin` in the API keys section or with
`cli.bat users api-key --username U --name N`, and the client sends it as
`Authorization: Bearer tt-…`. Keys carry the user's role, never expire, and
are revoked from `/admin` or with `users api-key-revoke --prefix P`; only
their SHA-256 is stored and the plaintext is shown once at creation.
Uploads stay
`multipart/form-data`; only the response format changes. Send
`Accept: application/json` (or `?format=json`) to get JSON instead of the
browser `303` redirect. Error responses use the same HTTP status codes with a
`{"error": "..."}` body. Anonymous JSON clients get `401`; logged-in users
without the role get `403`. Reading is public, like the library pages, except
locked-list videos (see above); writing
requires the matching role.

| Method | Route | Auth | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `POST` | `/language` | none | Form fields `language= ` (initially `en` or `el`) and optional site-local `next`; saves the browser language and redirects back. Same-origin protection applies. |
| `POST` | `/api/login` | none | JSON `{"username", "password"}`; sets the session cookie, returns `{"username", "role"}`. |
| `POST` | `/logout` | session | Revokes the session cookie. |
| `POST` | `/api/upload` | editor | Multipart fields `title` (required), `desc`, `category`, `file`, `access_list` (empty for public, otherwise a locked-list id). JSON clients get `201` with `id`, `title`, `status`, `original`, `access_list`, `watch_url`, `video_url`, `api_url`. Browsers get `303` to `/watch?id=`. |
| `GET` | `/view_list?key=…` | none | HTML page with exactly one locked list's videos; grants an unlock cookie. Without `key`, shows everything the cookie already unlocked. Unknown keys return 404. |
| `GET` | `/api/videos?q=&category=&page=1&page_size=50` | none | JSON fields `total`, `filtered`, `count`, `page`, `page_size`, `pages`, `q`, `category`, `sort`, and `items`, with the same filtering as the library page. Locked videos are excluded unless `?key=…`, an unlock cookie, or an editor/administrator credential is presented. `total` counts all visible videos; `filtered` counts matches; `count` counts this page's items. Use `sort=views` for view count or `sort=title` for title; the default is recency. |
| `GET` | `/api/video?id= ` | none | JSON metadata for one video, including `status` (`queued`/`processing`/`ready`/`failed`), `access_list` and `views`. `404` when missing or locked without access. |
| `POST` | `/api/edit` | editor | Form fields `id`, `title`, `desc`, `category`, `access_list`. JSON clients get `200` with `id`, `title`, `watch_url`, `api_url`. |
| `POST` | `/api/delete` | admin | Form field `id`. JSON clients get `200` with `{"id", "deleted": true}`. |

Poll `GET /api/video?id= ` until `status` is `ready` (or `failed`), then
open `watch_url`. Serve over HTTPS when credentials cross a network; the Go
server itself serves HTTP (see the Nginx example).

```sh
curl -c session.txt -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"secret"}' http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/login
curl -b session.txt -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -F title="Demo" -F desc="Recorded meeting" -F category="Meetings" \
  -F file=@demo.mp4 http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/upload
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/video?id=<id>"
```

With an API key instead of the session cookie:

```sh
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer tt-..." -H "Accept: application/json" \
  -F title="Demo" -F desc="Recorded meeting" -F category="Meetings" \
  -F file=@demo.mp4 http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/upload
```

```python
import os
import requests
base = "http://127.0.0.1:8081"
s = requests.Session()
s.post(f"{base}/api/login",
    json={"username": "admin", "password": os.environ["ADMIN_PASS"]}).raise_for_status()
with open("demo.mp4", "rb") as f:
    r = s.post(f"{base}/api/upload",
        headers={"Accept": "application/json"},
        data={"title": "Demo", "desc": "Recorded meeting", "category": "Meetings"},
        files={"file": ("demo.mp4", f, "video/mp4")})
r.raise_for_status()
video_id = r.json()["id"]
print(requests.get(f"{base}/api/video", params={"id": video_id}).json())
```

## Storage and conversion

SQLite uses the pure Go `modernc.org/sqlite` driver, so single-binary builds do
not require CGO. Legacy filesystem JSON metadata remains available with `STORE=fs`.

```text
videos/
  tiny-tube.db       # SQLite metadata; WAL/SHM files may also exist
  <id>/
    original.mp4     # or .mov, .mkv, .webm
    meta.json        # legacy FS mode, or retained migration source
    hls-<generated>/ # published after successful conversion
      index.m3u8
      seg000.ts
      poster.jpg     # optional preview frame
      ...
```

HLS currently has a single rendition scaled to 720 pixels high, H.264 video,
AAC audio, and a target segment duration of six seconds. It is not adaptive
multi-quality streaming. Originals are kept after conversion.

Original files support HTTP Range requests, but seeking also depends on the file
layout and browser. The code does not apply MP4 `faststart` to originals. Multipart
file parts use at most an 8 MiB memory threshold before spilling to temporary disk;
the separate request limit is enforced by `http.MaxBytesReader`.

Existing videos, including root-level `index.m3u8` and `poster.jpg`, remain compatible.
SQLite startup imports legacy `meta.json` records whose IDs are absent from the
database. Repeated imports leave existing SQLite edits untouched. JSON files are
retained; switching back to `STORE=fs` does not export later SQLite edits. Existing
SQLite databases are upgraded to retain conversion error messages and add
user/session tables without losing rows.
In FS mode, metadata is written to a temporary file, synced/closed, and replaced.
Application reads and writes use in-process synchronization. Run **one server process per video
directory**; shared storage across multiple instances is not supported.

## Optional Nginx deployment

Go can serve everything itself. nginx.sample.conf proxies all
routes, including `/videos/`, through Go so its private-file and link checks apply.
Range/206 and HLS/poster content types are preserved. It is a starting point,
not a complete deployment configuration:

- Replace the sample hostname and storage path, and configure TLS certificates;
 the configured files must exist before Nginx can start.
- The sample has a 2 GiB whole-request cap and 300-second inactivity timeouts.
 Keep the proxy cap consistent if changing `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`. Upload request
 buffering is disabled to avoid an additional full copy at the proxy.
- Restrict direct access to the Go port when TLS/auth routing relies on the proxy.
- Go already checks session roles. Additional Nginx upload authentication is
 optional and must not break the session cookie if enabled.
- Keep SQLite files and their journals private. The example blocks database
 extensions and staging paths; Go also checks file identities to reject DB aliases.
 Its upstream uses the default port 8081; adjust it if changing `ADDR`/`PORT`.

Capacity has not been measured. Validate the edited configuration with `nginx -t`
on the deployment machine, then check a real authenticated upload and playback.

## Development

### Run and build from source

In a source checkout, install patched Go 1.26.10 or 1.27.3+; `go.mod` selects
Go 1.27.3. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set the first administrator password
as described in Installation. Then run
`go run .` from the repository directory, or build an executable:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
go build -o tiny-tube.exe .
.\tiny-tube.exe
```

```sh
# Linux / macOS
go build -o tiny-tube .
./tiny-tube
```

On Windows, `dev.bat` (or `.\dev.bat` in PowerShell) can rebuild and restart
the application as source files, assets, catalogs, module files, or `.env` change.
For the administration CLI, use `cli.bat` or `go run ./cmd/cli` with the same
storage settings as the server. The tracked video under `testdata/` is a test
fixture, not library content.

To cross-build a Linux binary from Windows PowerShell, choose the target's
architecture:

```powershell
$env:GOOS = "linux"
$env:GOARCH = "amd64" # or arm64
go build -o tiny-tube .
Remove-Item Env:GOOS, Env:GOARCH
```

### Tests and CI

GitHub Actions runs CI for every push and pull request,
and can also be started manually from the Actions tab:

- Go tests on Linux and Windows, with real FFmpeg installed so HLS/poster tests run.
- Linux race detection, shuffled uncached tests, coverage reports retained for
 seven days, and CGO-free builds on both platforms.
- `gofmt` for changed Go files (matching the scoped-formatting policy), `go vet`,
 module checksum verification and `go mod tidy -diff`.
- The Node UI behavior suite and syntax checks for embedded JavaScript.
- Pinned `govulncheck` scans for Linux, Windows and macOS using the live vulnerability
 database. Database/tool failures fail the job; they are not treated as a pass.

Pushing a version tag such as `v1.0` or `v1.0.1` runs these same checks first,
then cross-builds six CGO-free platform packages and publishes a GitHub Release
with all archives and `SHA256SUMS`. A failed check or platform build blocks release
publication. Linux/Windows tests execute natively; macOS and ARM packages are
cross-compiled, without native runtime tests for every target. Ordinary branch
pushes and pull requests do not publish releases.

Actions are pinned to commit SHAs, repository permissions default to read-only, jobs
have time limits, and superseded branch runs are cancelled. CI uses the Go
toolchain selected in `go.mod`. Only the final release job has permission to
publish downloads. It does not deploy the application. Branch
protection/required checks must be configured separately in repository settings.

```sh
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go build ./...
```

Tests cover concurrent uploads, request limits, cleanup, metadata replacement,
authentication, HTTP playback/Range support, bounded conversion concurrency, and
shutdown/restart recovery, both storage backends, schema/import migration, and
editing/deleting during conversion. A real FFmpeg upload-to-HLS integration test runs when
FFmpeg is on `PATH`, and is skipped otherwise.

`GET /healthz` reports liveness. `GET /readyz` checks writable storage and readable
metadata, returning 503 if either fails; it does not certify FFmpeg codecs or disk
capacity. For manual verification, check search, authenticated upload, conversion,
and browser playback. Use a temporary `VIDEO_DIR` for checks that modify storage.

Contributor guidance is in AGENTS.md. Runtime uploads are ignored by
Git; only the fixture under `testdata/` remains tracked. Back up video files and
the SQLite database, including a custom external `DB_PATH`. Stop the server before
copying a SQLite database, or use SQLite's backup facility; copying only the live
`.db` file may omit uncheckpointed WAL changes. There is no built-in quota,
recovery or backup mechanism.

HTML templates, styles, and scripts live under `web/` and are embedded in the Go
executable. No frontend package installation or separate asset deployment is
needed. Rebuild/restart the server after editing these files.

The post-merge security check and its deployment limitations are recorded in
docs/SECURITY.md. Keep video/database storage writable only by
the service account, run FFmpeg with minimal OS privileges, use HTTPS for network
access, and rebuild existing binaries with the selected patched toolchain.

The 2026-10-24 review and resolutions records
the additional fixes. Run `node --test tests/ui.test.cjs` for the client-behavior
suite (Node is a test tool, not a runtime dependency).
